statement: Avoid deep sedation unless clinically required.
synthesis: PADIS 2018 directly supports the statement: it suggests light over deep sedation in critically ill, mechanically ventilated adults and advises clinicians to target a light rather than deep level of sedation unless deeper sedation is clinically indicated — this on-scope recommendation governs. The 2025 focused update did not re-address the sedation-depth question (it re-examined dexmedetomidine vs propofol and added anxiety), so the 2018 light-sedation recommendation remains the current position, while the ICUDelirium.org SAT/SBT page corroborates the light-sedation goal via a specific titration method rather than the depth recommendation itself.

perSource.note: Governing on-scope source: the guideline's Light Sedation recommendation directly endorses light over deep sedation and states the target-light-unless-clinically-indicated principle the claim paraphrases.

statement: Daily SAT/SBT when feasible.
synthesis: The archived ICUDelirium (Wake Up and Breathe / ABC study) page is the on-scope source and governs the claim: it directly pairs daily SATs with daily SBTs within a protocol of safety screens and failure criteria, which is exactly "daily SAT/SBT when feasible." PADIS 2018 partially aligns — it endorses the daily SAT (DSI) as one of two equivalent (ungraded) ways to reach light sedation and notes light sedation is needed to enable SBTs, but does not itself issue the paired SAT+SBT recommendation — and the 2025 focused update did not revisit this question (its sedation update is sedative drug choice only), so the 2018 position remains the current guideline position.

statement: Positive — delirium present
synthesis: Both sources agree and are on-scope for the adult ICU: the CAM-ICU Worksheet's decision rule and Ely 2001 (the CAM-ICU validation study) each state that when Features 1 and 2 plus either Feature 3 or 4 are present the patient is delirious (CAM positive), directly supporting "Positive — delirium present." No source contradicts or narrows the claim.

statement: Negative
synthesis: Both sources agree. The CAM-ICU Worksheet is the operational instrument for the status-strip result and explicitly yields "Not Delirious" (the Negative result) whenever the feature combination for delirium is not met, and Ely 2001 validates the identical algorithm — delirious only with Features 1 and 2 plus either 3 or 4, otherwise the Overall CAM-ICU Assessment is answered "No" — with a 98-100% negative predictive value. The Worksheet governs the "Negative" label and Ely 2001 concurs and validates it, with no scope conflict.

statement: Unable to assess (RASS −4/−5)
synthesis: Ely 2001 is the governing on-scope source: it defines RASS -4 (responds only to physical/painful stimulation) and -5 (no response) as unarousable states and validated the CAM-ICU only in patients arousable to voice, explicitly excluding comatose and stuporous evaluations because they lack characteristic delirium features — the clinical basis for reporting "unable to assess" at RASS -4/-5. The provided CAM-ICU Worksheet extraction references RASS only within Features 1 and 3 and omits any preliminary sedation-gate step, so it does not state this rule; the operational "stop and reassess later" threshold is standard CAM-ICU flowsheet practice consistent with Ely 2001's validation population.

perSource.cite: Ely EW, Inouye SK, Bernard GR, et al. Delirium in mechanically ventilated patients: validity and reliability of the CAM-ICU. JAMA. 2001;286(21):2703-2710.
perSource.note: Governing on-scope source: defines RASS -4/-5 as unarousable and validated CAM-ICU only in verbally-arousable patients (comatose/stuporous excluded), the basis for 'unable to assess' — but does not print the operational status label verbatim.

statement: Hyperactive (agitated, combative — least common)
synthesis: la Cour 2022, a systematic scoping review of 131 ICU studies, is the governing on-scope source: among studies reporting all three motor subtypes, hyperactive delirium was the least prevalent (22.7%), below hypoactive (50.3%) and mixed (27.7%), directly supporting "hyperactive — least common," and it describes the subtype as agitated/aggressive/restless. Krewulak 2018 (unarchived, cited) is concordant per la Cour, while Hayhurst 2020 is a nearest match at a different scope — a single cohort using a two-way, non-exclusive hypo/hyper scheme that confirms only that hyperactive is less common than hypoactive (17% vs 71%) and never addresses the mixed subtype, so it does not independently establish the three-way "least common" ranking.

statement: Hypoactive (somnolent, quiet — most common, easily missed)
synthesis: la Cour 2022 (systematic scoping review, 131 ICU studies, 50,232 patients) and Hayhurst 2020 (582-patient ICU cohort) agree that hypoactive delirium — reduced activity, apathy, hypersomnolence, the 'somnolent, quiet' presentation — is the most common ICU motor subtype (50.3% pooled prevalence; 71% vs 17% vs hyperactive in Hayhurst) and frequently goes undiagnosed without routine screening ('easily missed'). la Cour governs the 'most common' assertion as the pooled-review source and the primary anchor, while Hayhurst supplies the 'easily missed' support; note that Hayhurst's postoperative/hospital-settings sentence is a different-setting nearest match about complications/mortality, not prevalence, and should not be read as direct support.

statement: Mixed (fluctuates between both)
synthesis: la Cour 2022 governs this claim: it directly defines the mixed motor subtype both conceptually ("the patient shifts between hyperactive and hypoactive delirium") and operationally ("any combination of hypo- and hyperactive delirium assessments during ICU stay") in adult critically ill patients, matching the tool's "Mixed (fluctuates between both)." Krewulak 2018 (not archived) is cited as the adult-ICU subtype incidence/prevalence review that recognizes mixed as a subtype, while Hayhurst 2020 is a nearest match at a different scope — it studies subtype cognitive outcomes and deliberately counts days with both subtypes instead of labeling patients "mixed," so it is background context rather than direct support.

statement: D — Drugs / Withdrawal: Deliriogenic agents? Dose reduction? Alcohol / benzo / opioid withdrawal — check last use & home meds.
synthesis: The archived Vanderbilt/CIBS Terminology & Mnemonics page directly supports the claim: the DELIRIUM(S) (SLU GEMS) mnemonic the tool reproduces lists 'D — Drugs,' and the same page's ICU DELIRIUM(S) 'D rugs' entry supplies the deliriogenic-agent and withdrawal detail (benzodiazepines/opiates, anticholinergics, alcohol/smoking cessation, withdrawal from chronically used sedatives) that the tool's statement expands on, with Flaherty 2011 and Maldonado 2018 cited as corroborating drug/withdrawal etiology; this on-scope DELIRIUM(S) mnemonic governs. Nearest-match passages that share the drug keyword but sit at a different scope — Dr. DRE 'Drug Removal' (a management/intervention mnemonic) and I WATCH DEATH 'Withdrawal' (a broader all-setting differential) — should not be read as the causative DELIRIUM(S) list, and explicit 'opioid withdrawal' is a modest extension since the page names opiates only as deliriogenic drugs.

statement: Verbal reorientation each encounter
synthesis: PADIS 2018 governs on-scope: it is the only source that directly supports the ICU claim, recommending a multicomponent nonpharmacologic intervention in critically ill adults and explicitly naming reorientation (with clocks and cognitive stimulation) among the delirium-reduction strategies, while the SCCM ICU Liberation bundle and Pun 2019 situate this within the ICU 'D' (Delirium: assess, prevent, manage) element without itemizing reorientation. statement: No antipsychotics at discharge without a psychiatric indication.
synthesis: The two on-scope guideline sources agree and govern: PADIS 2018 (the primary anchor) states antipsychotics started for ICU delirium often remain on unnecessarily after discharge, and the 2025 PADIS focused update explicitly advises discontinuing ICU-initiated antipsychotics upon discharge if no longer clinically required — together directly supporting "no antipsychotics at discharge without a psychiatric indication." The other four sources are supporting context of a different scope and must not be read as direct support: MIND-USA supplies the efficacy basis (haloperidol/ziprasidone did not alter delirium duration), the haloperidol label gives the general safety rationale (tardive-dyskinesia risk rising with duration; reassess continued need), and the dexmedetomidine label and MENDS2 concern sedation choice/dosing rather than antipsychotic de-prescribing.

statement: Bolus over continuous: When safe, consider intermittent dosing rather than continuous infusions.
synthesis: The bedside heuristic to prefer intermittent dosing over continuous infusions when safe is directionally consistent with PADIS 2018's sedation-minimization framework, but PADIS 2018 — the only on-scope source — explicitly treats the intermittent-vs-continuous comparison as an evidence gap that "needs to be studied" rather than issuing a graded recommendation, so its support is partial. The other three sources are nearest matches on different questions (PADIS 2025 and MENDS2 address sedative agent choice among continuous infusions; SAT/SBT addresses daily sedative interruption), none of which evaluate delivery mode, so PADIS 2018 remains the governing (though non-graded) source for this claim.

statement: Daily SAT / SBT: Awakening + breathing trial daily when feasible; coordinate with respiratory therapy.
synthesis: The governing on-scope source is the Vanderbilt CIBS "Both SAT and SBT" reference, which—drawing on the ABC/Wake Up and Breathe trial—supports pairing daily spontaneous awakening trials with daily spontaneous breathing trials in one coordinated protocol. PADIS 2018 backs the daily SAT (DSI) component and states light sedation is needed to facilitate SBTs, but frames SAT as one of two equivalent titration methods rather than issuing the pairing/coordination recommendation itself, so it is partial; MENDS2 2021 applied SAT/SBT coordination only as background ABCDE-bundle adherence within a dexmedetomidine-versus-propofol trial in septic patients (a different intervention), and the 2025 PADIS focused update did not re-address SAT/SBT, so the 2018 position remains the current guideline stance.

statement: CAM-ICU & RASS each shift: Document RASS; complete the CAM-ICU once per shift and with any mental-status change.
synthesis: PADIS 2018 governs and directly supports the statement: its good practice statements that critically ill adults be regularly assessed for delirium with a valid tool and that sedation status be frequently reassessed with valid and reliable scales underwrite documenting RASS and completing the CAM-ICU as routine monitoring — though the specific "once per shift and with any mental-status change" cadence is a common ABCDEF-bundle operationalization rather than a verbatim guideline number. The 2025 focused update did not re-address monitoring frequency, so the 2018 statements remain the current position; MENDS2 (a sepsis-restricted sedative-choice RCT using twice-daily research assessments) and the SAT/SBT page (sedative titration/ventilator liberation) are nearest matches on different scope, not monitoring recommendations.

statement: Multimodal pain management: Analgesia first — scheduled acetaminophen, NSAIDs where appropriate, regional techniques to limit opioids.
synthesis: PADIS 2018 is the governing on-scope source and directly supports the statement: it endorses an analgesia-first, multimodal strategy with acetaminophen as a scheduled opioid-sparing adjunct, nonopioids combined with regional anesthetics to spare opioids, and NSAIDs used only where appropriate (advising against routine adjunctive NSAIDs for nonprocedural pain while endorsing them as an opioid alternative for discrete procedures). The 2025 focused update did not re-address the pain/analgesia questions, so the 2018 recommendation remains the current position; Beers 2023 aligns in a different (older-adult) population, and the two melatonin sources do not bear on pain management.

statement: Review medications daily: Can any deliriogenic drug be stopped or reduced? Benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, steroids.
synthesis: Beers 2023 is the governing on-scope source and directly backs the claim's specific triad, naming benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, and corticosteroids (oral and parenteral) as delirium-precipitating drugs to avoid or minimize during medication review, while PADIS 2018 corroborates the benzodiazepine element for the ICU (a modifiable delirium risk factor; prefer propofol/dexmedetomidine) but does not address anticholinergics or steroids. The 2025 PADIS focused update did not re-address deliriogenic-medication review, so these positions remain the current guidance (with a caveat not to abruptly stop chronic benzodiazepines), whereas the two melatonin sources describe a different prevention intervention and do not support the deprescribing action.

statement: Treat pain before sedation: Uncontrolled pain drives agitation — assess and treat pain first.
synthesis: PADIS 2018 directly and cleanly supports the actionable directive: its good practice statement holds that ICU pain "should be treated before a sedative agent is considered," and the analgosedation recommendation makes "treating pain a priority over providing sedatives" (the analgesia-first principle) — while the rationale clause "uncontrolled pain drives agitation" is not a stated general guideline finding (PADIS only notes agitation "may have been pain related" in commentary on one dexmedetomidine trial), so that clause is background rationale rather than a cited conclusion. The 2025 focused update did not re-address the analgesia-first / pain-before-sedation question, so the 2018 statement remains the current position; Beers 2023, Pro-MEDIC 2022, and the 2025 melatonin meta-analysis are cited for other Pain/Pharmacy-card content and are silent on treating pain before sedation.

statement: Avoid meperidine: Higher neurotoxicity/delirium risk than other opioids (Beers) — avoid in at-risk patients.
synthesis: Beers 2023 is the governing on-scope source and directly supports the claim, listing meperidine among opioids to avoid because it "may have a higher risk of neurotoxicity, including delirium, than other opioids," with the opioid class now folded into its delirium drug-disease criterion (avoid in older adults with or at high risk of delirium). PADIS 2018's nearest content — that opioid use as a class is strongly shown not to alter ICU delirium risk — is a different-scope question (a whole-class ICU risk-factor analysis, not one drug's relative neurotoxicity in older adults) and does not contradict Beers; PADIS 2025 does not re-address it, so PADIS 2018 remains the current position, while Pro-MEDIC and the melatonin meta-analysis are melatonin studies unrelated to meperidine.

statement: Melatonin — consider for prevention: PADIS 2025 conditionally suggests melatonin to reduce delirium (low-certainty evidence); dose per local practice.
synthesis: The on-scope primary source, PADIS 2025, directly supports the claim: it issues a conditional recommendation (for intervention; low certainty) to administer melatonin in adult ICU patients, grounded in a possible reduction in delirium prevalence (RR 0.70), and explicitly declines a specific dose because of trial heterogeneity — matching "dose per local practice." statement: Glasses, hearing aids, orient: Sensory deprivation is reversible; update the orientation board every shift.

statement: Dexmedetomidine preferred in ventilated patients — reduces delirium vs benzodiazepines; monitor bradycardia / hypotension.
synthesis: PADIS 2025 is the governing on-scope source and supports the statement's clinical substance: dexmedetomidine is preferred over propofol for sedation in ventilated ICU adults where reducing delirium is a priority (delirium RR 0.55), with an increased bradycardia risk and a hypotension caveat to monitor. The claim's "vs benzodiazepines" framing traces to the 2018 PADIS recommendation (dexmedetomidine OR propofol over benzodiazepines), which the 2025 focused update did not re-address and so remains the current position — but the 2025 quantified delirium reduction is vs propofol, and MENDS2 (dexmedetomidine vs propofol in sepsis) found no delirium/coma-free difference, so none of these sources demonstrates a benzodiazepine-comparator delirium reduction; Haloperidol PI, Hodgson 2014, and the early-mobility page are different-intervention references bundled into the Sedation section, not support for this statement.

statement: Haloperidol for hyperactive delirium with safety risk — baseline EKG, monitor QTc; IV route off-label, prefer PO/IM; avoid in Parkinson / Lewy body disease.
synthesis: The Haloperidol prescribing information is the on-scope source and directly supports each safety element in the statement: IV administration and high doses raise QTc-prolongation/Torsades risk with ECG monitoring required (basis for baseline EKG / monitor QTc), IV is not an approved route (off-label) while IM is the labeled parenteral route with oral to supplant it (prefer PO/IM), and haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia — so the label governs the claim. statement: Apply S·P·A on admission

PADIS 2025 agrees at the level of individual ICU domains (sedation, mobilization, pharmacology) but as a focused update does not restate the on-admission-for-all timing, and Project BETA is a nearest keyword match on the escalation-ladder topic but a different scope (verbal de-escalation of agitated patients, not on-admission prevention).

statement: Lowest dose, shortest duration; monitor QTc
synthesis: NICE CG103 (p.11) is the governing on-scope source: it directly supports the lowest clinically appropriate dose and short-term haloperidol (usually 1 week or less), reserved for delirium patients who are a risk to self/others after de-escalation fails, and cautions about cardiac side effects — the basis for QTc monitoring, though it does not use the words "monitor QTc." PADIS 2025 (ICU antipsychotics-for-delirium, which declines to recommend and reports only pooled QT/arrhythmia safety data) and Project BETA (emergency-psychiatry agitation, medication-as-last-resort) are nearest matches at different scope that reinforce the surrounding framing but do not state the lowest-dose/shortest-duration/monitor-QTc rule.

Support is partial only on wording: the card's descriptor "Spontaneous attention to caregiver" is a behavioral gloss of that alert-and-calm level and appears nowhere verbatim in the source (whose RASS-0 term, per both Kerson and the cited Sessler 2002 original, is "Alert and calm").

statement: CAPD — Every age — the default screen: Observational: rate the child over the shift against age-expected behavior. Works at any developmental age, including deep developmental delay.
synthesis: Traube 2014 is the on-scope governing source: it developed and validated the CAPD as a rapid observational nursing screen scored over the shift against per-developmental-stage anchor points, across ages 0–21 and all developmental levels, retaining high sensitivity (96.2%) and applicability (AUC 0.86) in developmentally delayed children — though nurses became adept "in all but the most developmentally delayed patients" and specificity fell to 51.2%, a caveat on the claim's "including deep developmental delay" wording. Smith 2016 corroborates CAPD's characterization ("subjective scoring over a nursing shift" with anchor points for each developmental stage) but its own psCAM-ICU is a different-scope tool (interactive/objective, ages 6mo–5yr, and it explicitly excluded deep developmental delay), and Smith 2011's pCAM-ICU is the ≥5-years cooperation-required alternative — both are the contrast screens on the "choose-the-screen" card, not support for CAPD's every-age/deep-delay applicability.

statement: Withdrawal can mimic delirium — if the child is on or weaning prolonged opioids or benzodiazepines, assess for iatrogenic withdrawal (e.g. WAT-1).
synthesis: The SCCM PANDEM 2022 guideline is the on-scope source and directly supports the claim on both counts: it states that the nonspecific symptoms of iatrogenic withdrawal syndrome (whose CNS features explicitly include delirium) can prevent identification of delirium, and it recommends the Withdrawal Assessment Tool-1 (or Sophia Observation Scale) for assessing opioid- or benzodiazepine-related withdrawal in critically ill children who are on or weaning prolonged exposure. The remaining cited sources are silent on withdrawal-as-mimic — the delirium screens (CAPD, psCAM-ICU, pCAM-ICU) and sedation scales (SBS, RASS) are the card's general assessment citations, and Mody 2018 addresses benzodiazepine exposure as a delirium risk factor rather than withdrawal from benzodiazepines mimicking delirium — so PANDEM 2022 governs.

statement: Tell the team on rounds: target arousal, actual arousal, screen result, and today’s plan.
synthesis: PANDEM 2022 is the governing pediatric guideline and supports the card's rounds prompt piece by piece — it recommends a validated daily target sedation depth (target arousal), sedation scales (SBS/COMFORT-B/RASS) for actual arousal, routine delirium screening for the screen result, and interdisciplinary rounds as the venue — while the instrument papers (Sessler RASS, Curley SBS, Traube CAPD, Smith ps/pCAM-ICU) validate the specific tools that generate those reported values and Mody supports the benzodiazepine "fix." statement: Find and fix precipitants: pain, hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic derangement, new medications.
synthesis: The on-scope governing source is SCCM PANDEM 2022, which recommends that initial delirium management focus on identifying and treating underlying etiologies via the BRAIN MAPS differential (Bring oxygen, Remove deliriogenic drugs, New organ dysfunction, Metabolic disturbances, Pain), directly matching the claim's precipitant list; Gupta 2021 concurs generally (treatment = environmental modification plus addressing the underlying trigger) and Mody 2018 substantiates the single 'new medications' element via benzodiazepines. The remaining sources (Traube, Smith 2016, Curley, and the RASS/pCAM-ICU citations) are different-scope — they validate detection/sedation instruments rather than the act-on-a-positive management step.

statement: Switch benzodiazepine sedation to dexmedetomidine; target light, goal-directed sedation.
synthesis: The pediatric guideline SCCM PANDEM 2022 governs and directly supports all three elements of the statement: it recommends alpha2-agonists (dexmedetomidine) as the primary sedative class, recommends minimizing benzodiazepine-based sedation to reduce delirium, and recommends assigning a validated, targeted (goal-directed) depth of sedation, with its rationale explicitly endorsing "transition to dexmedetomidine sedation." Mody 2018 supplies the pediatric causal, dose-dependent benzodiazepine-to-delirium evidence underpinning the benzodiazepine-sparing half; the RASS/SBS sedation scales and the CAPD/pCAM/psCAM delirium screens share keywords but are different-scope (they are the measurement and detection instruments that operationalize monitoring and trigger the bundle, not evidence for the sedative switch), and PANDEM's dexmedetomidine-specific evidence draws partly on a post-operative cardiac/scoliosis and adult-RCT base.

statement: Deprescribe anticholinergics; minimize restraints.
synthesis: The governing on-scope source is the 2022 SCCM PANDEM pediatric guideline, whose BRAIN MAPS delirium-management model directs clinicians to "Remove/Reduce deliriogenic drugs" and address "Immobilization" — the broader categories the card operationalizes as "deprescribe anticholinergics" and "minimize restraints." Mody 2018 (critically ill children, same PICU population) partially corroborates the restraint side — restraint use was a highly significant bivariate predictor of delirium (52% vs 18%, p<0.001) — but names anticholinergics only as an unstudied plausible contributor (a stated limitation), and the remaining citations are the card's screening instruments (RASS, SBS, CAPD, Gupta, pCAM/psCAM) that are silent on this intervention.

statement: Restore sleep and day–night rhythm; mobilize early; maximize family presence.
synthesis: SCCM PANDEM 2022 is the governing on-scope source and directly supports all three limbs of the statement: it recommends optimizing sleep hygiene with day–night cycling, facilitating family presence/involvement, and performing early mobility (EM) to reduce delirium in critically ill children. statement: Drugs treat symptoms only — if agitation threatens safety and non-pharm has failed, consider a short course of an antipsychotic (PANDEM prefers no agent; atypicals are usually chosen first in reported PICU practice) at the lowest effective dose, reassessed daily (off-label, limited evidence).
synthesis: The 2022 SCCM PANDEM pediatric guideline governs and directly supports the statement: it does not suggest routine antipsychotics (prefers no agent) but suggests haloperidol or an atypical antipsychotic be considered for refractory/severe delirium at the smallest effective dose after nonpharmacologic measures, noting antipsychotics do not treat the cause and are FDA off-label in children; Gupta 2021 (single-center PICU) agrees, reserving antipsychotics (risperidone, then haloperidol) for refractory cases. Mody 2018 is a nearest match on drugs and pediatric delirium but a different intervention (benzodiazepines as a deliriogenic risk factor, not antipsychotic treatment), and the RASS/SBS/CAPD/pCAM screening sources support assessment rather than pharmacologic escalation.

statement: Before and during any antipsychotic: baseline 12-lead ECG (QTc), electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca), review of QT-prolonging drugs.
synthesis: SCCM PANDEM 2022 is the governing on-scope source and directly supports the claim's core: it strongly recommends a baseline electrocardiogram followed by routine electrolyte and QTc-interval monitoring for critically ill children receiving haloperidol or atypical antipsychotics, with a rationale citing cardiac side effects. statement: C — Choice of analgesia & sedation: Light, goal-directed (SBS −1 to 0 / unit RASS target); minimize benzodiazepines, prefer dexmedetomidine.
synthesis: The on-scope sources agree. The SCCM PANDEM 2022 pediatric guideline governs and directly supports all three elements of the statement: light, goal-directed sedation (assign and target a validated sedation depth), minimizing benzodiazepine-based sedation, and preferring alpha2-agonists/dexmedetomidine as the primary sedative class; Mody 2018 independently supplies causal dose-response evidence for benzodiazepine minimization in critically ill children, and Curley 2006 grounds the SBS -1 to 0 scale used as the pediatric light-sedation target (RASS, from the adult-derived Sessler 2002, is the adult analog). statement: D — Delirium: assess, prevent & manage: Screen at least each shift with CAPD or pCAM/psCAM; address precipitants.
synthesis: The governing on-scope source is the 2022 SCCM PANDEM guideline (Table 1, p. e77), which recommends the ps/pCAM-ICU or CAPD as the most valid and reliable delirium monitoring tools, routine screening from ICU admission through discharge, and identifying/modifying precipitants (BRAIN MAPS) — covering both halves of the claim; the tool-validation papers agree (Traube 2014 for CAPD, Smith 2016 for the psCAM-ICU, with Smith 2011/pCAM-ICU cited but unarchived), and Traube 2014 is the specific source of the "at least each shift" frequency ("a minimum of twice daily, once by each shift nurse"), which PANDEM itself does not quantify, while Mody 2018 supports "address precipitants" by identifying benzodiazepines as a modifiable precipitant. Two nearest-match sources differ in scope and drive the discrepancy: Gupta 2021 evaluates CAPD only in mechanically ventilated/sedated children and reports poor specificity (44.8% overall; 16.5% with developmental delay), a subgroup caveat rather than a contradiction, and Curley 2006 validates the State Behavioral Scale, a sedation/arousal instrument (not a delirium tool) that serves only as the arousal gate before delirium scoring.

statement: E — Early mobility & exercise: Developmentally appropriate (passive ROM → active play → sit → stand → ambulate); involve PT/OT/child-life.
synthesis: SCCM PANDEM 2022 is the only on-scope source and governs this card: it recommends performing early mobility to minimize immobility and using a standardized EM protocol with "developmentally appropriate mobility activities" and "progressive levels of mobility activities" guided by the multidisciplinary team, and it names physical and occupational therapists as the EM-relevant disciplines — supporting the developmentally-graded progression and PT/OT involvement, though the specific step sequence (passive ROM to active play to sit to stand to ambulate) operationalizes the guideline's general "developmentally appropriate/progressive" language rather than appearing verbatim, and child life appears in PANDEM only as a research question on environmental comfort, not as an EM component. The remaining sources are delirium/sedation assessment tools (SBS, CAPD, psCAM-ICU) and a benzodiazepine study that do not address early mobility as an intervention; their "sit/climb out of bed," "play/crawl or walk," "child life," and "mobilization" wording is different-scope keyword overlap (scale item design, developmental anchor points, developmental-age assessment, and an analgosedation downstream benefit), not direct support.

statement: F — Family engagement & empowerment: Caregiver presence, comfort, familiar voice/objects; educate families to recognize delirium.
synthesis: SCCM PANDEM 2022 is the only on-scope source and it supports the claim: it recommends family engagement on rounds and in direct care, conditionally recommends facilitating parental/caregiver presence to provide comfort, and states that familiar care team members and comforting objects from home help reorient patients — so it governs and remains the current position. The 'educate families to recognize delirium' component is only partially anchored (the guideline lists family communication/empowerment as a research gap rather than a graded recommendation), and the screening-tool papers (Curley SBS, Traube CAPD, Gupta, Smith psCAM-ICU) and the benzodiazepine study (Mody) share keywords like caregiver voice, familiar objects, and parents/caregivers only inside tool items or citations, making them different-scope rather than support.

statement: Protect sleep / circadian rhythm — cluster night care, reduce noise and light, avoid sleep-fragmenting sedatives.
synthesis: The primary source, the 2022 SCCM PANDEM pediatric guideline, directly and fully supports the statement: it recommends optimizing sleep hygiene and maintaining day/night cycles (minimizing noise, light, and stimulation), reducing excessive ambient noise, limiting sleep-disrupting frequent caregiver assessments, and minimizing benzodiazepine-based sedation, all as PICU delirium-prevention measures — so PANDEM governs and remains the current position. Mody 2018 narrowly reinforces only the "avoid sedatives" clause (benzodiazepines in PICU children, on delirium-causation grounds rather than sleep-fragmentation), while the screening-instrument papers (Curley SBS, Traube CAPD, Gupta, Smith psCAM, Sessler RASS, Smith pCAM) do not state this prevention measure — they touch sleep/environment only as a delirium diagnostic feature, a screening-timing note, or a general treatment aside, making them different-scope or background.

statement: Normalize day–night — daytime light and activity; dim, quiet nights; age-appropriate orientation.
synthesis: The governing source is SCCM PANDEM 2022 (environment domain, ~p. 16/e88-e89): its rationale directly supports the claim, recommending maintenance of day/night cycles with daytime light and activity, healthy quiet/dim sleep conditions at night, and reorientation via cognitive stimulation, familiar caregivers, and comforting objects. The other bundled citations do not address this environmental prevention measure and only overlap by keyword in a different scope — the scale-validation papers (SBS, CAPD, Gupta, psCAM-ICU) use "orientation"/"sleep-wake disturbance" as delirium assessment constructs, Gupta's "environmental modifications" describe post-diagnosis treatment, and Mody's delirium-prevention strategy is a different (pharmacologic, benzodiazepine-reduction) intervention.

statement: Sensory aids & engagement — glasses, hearing aids; familiar comfort objects, music, play, child-life.
synthesis: The primary anchor, SCCM PANDEM 2022 (p. 16 / e89), governs this claim and directly supports its engagement half — familiar comfort objects from home, family presence/involvement, and cognitive stimulation to reorient the child as low-risk nonpharmacologic delirium prevention — but it does not address the sensory-aid items (glasses, hearing aids) at all, and its music-therapy recommendation is for augmenting analgesia (pain), not delirium prevention. The remaining cited sources are screening/sedation-tool validations and a benzodiazepine risk-factor study that do not address this prevention measure; Traube 2014's "comforted by familiar objects" is a CAPD scoring anchor (a normal-behavior descriptor), not a prevention recommendation.

statement: Minimize restraints & deliriogenic meds — deprescribe anticholinergics; reduce physical restraints.
synthesis: The on-scope pediatric guideline (SCCM PANDEM 2022, p. 16/e89) governs and remains the current position: it supports minimizing deliriogenic medication via the BRAIN MAPS "Remove/Reduce deliriogenic drugs" model and a strong recommendation to minimize benzodiazepine-based sedation, and Mody 2018 corroborates in the same PICU population (benzodiazepines an independent, dose-dependent, modifiable risk factor; restraint use strongly associated with delirium; anticholinergics named as a further deliriogenic class). The cited PANDEM main text does not name "anticholinergics" or "physical restraints" specifically — that support comes from Mody 2018 — so PANDEM only partially covers the bullet, and the assessment/screening instruments (SBS, CAPD, psCAM-ICU, pCAM-ICU, RASS) are cited card-wide for detection, a different intervention scope than this prevention claim.

statement: Every PICU child, at least once per shift and with any mental-status change.
synthesis: The on-scope sources agree on universal, recurring screening: PANDEM 2022 recommends routine delirium screening of every critically ill child from admission through ICU discharge, while Traube 2014 (primary, p.8) and Traube 2017 set the cadence at twice daily / once by each shift nurse (Traube 2017 also cites the ESPNIC recommendation of every 8-12 hours). statement: Delirium is common (~25% point prevalence) and mostly hypoactive or mixed — easily missed without a screen.
synthesis: The sources agree that PICU delirium is common and predominantly hypoactive or mixed, and is easily missed without routine screening — the SCCM PANDEM 2022 guideline states this directly ("highly prevalent... with predominance of the hypoactive subtype which is most easily missed without routine screening") and governs the qualitative claim, concordant with Traube 2014 (20.6% prevalence), Traube 2017 (hypoactive 46%/mixed 45%, underdiagnosed without screening), and Smith 2016 psCAM-ICU (hypoactive predominant, easily undetected). Discrepancy to flag: the specific "~25% point prevalence" and the quoted "835 remaining subjects" passage come from Traube's International Point Prevalence Study (Crit Care Med 2017;45(4):584–590), but the file attached to the "Traube 2017" source is instead the single-center epidemiology/mortality study, which reports a lower 16.6% prevalence / 17.3% incidence — a citation-metadata mismatch that does not undercut the "mostly hypoactive/mixed, easily missed" portion but means no provided file contains the 25% figure verbatim.

statement: Comatose floor (RASS −4/−5 · SBS −2/−3) → record "unable to assess"; reassess when the child responds.
synthesis: The two on-scope validation sources agree directly: the psCAM-ICU (Smith 2016, the primary anchor) states a comatose child (RASS -4/-5) cannot be assessed for delirium and is recorded "unable to assess" (UTA), then only assessed once responsive to voice, and Traube 2017 defines the same daily "comatose" status (RASS -4/-5, unarousable, "impossible to assess for delirium"); Traube 2014 operationalizes the identical floor by excluding RASS < -3 from CAPD screening, and PANDEM 2022 endorses the gate at guideline level (the sedation/arousal score determines the appropriateness of delirium screening). The SBS half of the floor (SBS -2/-3) is grounded in Curley 2006, which defines those as the "Unresponsive"/"Responsive to noxious stimuli" levels but is a sedation-scale validation (narrower scope, not a delirium gate), so Smith 2016 governs the RASS floor while Curley 2006 supplies the SBS scale definition.

statement: psCAM-ICU — dev. age 6 mo–5 yr · pCAM-ICU — chronological and dev. age ≥ 5 yr: point-in-time interactive screens.
synthesis: The two on-scope sources agree and govern: the PANDEM 2022 guideline (primary) states the ps/pCAM-ICU are "point-in-time" assessments using observation and interactive components, with the pCAM-ICU validated in PICU patients over 5 years old and the psCAM-ICU adapted for children developmentally under 5, and Smith 2016 confirms the psCAM-ICU 6-month-to-5-year range plus the pCAM-ICU >5-year "in the moment" interactive design. statement: Positive: CAPD ≥ 9, or CAM Feature 1 + 2 + (3 or 4).
synthesis: The on-scope sources agree and jointly cover both halves of the rule: Traube 2014 (primary) validated CAPD >= 9 as the positive threshold (94% sensitivity / 79% specificity) and Traube 2017 restates "a CAPD score of 9 or higher represents a positive screen," while Smith 2016 (psCAM-ICU) defines the CAM algorithm as Feature 1 and Feature 2 plus either Feature 3 or 4 — together matching the claim exactly. PANDEM 2022 endorses the ps/pCAM-ICU and CAPD instruments at a broader tool-selection level rather than restating the cut points, and the nearest different-scope match, Curley 2006's State Behavioral Scale, is a sedation-assessment instrument (the arousal gate applied before screening), not a delirium-positivity rule.

statement: Negative → keep the prevention bundle going; rescreen next shift.
synthesis: The on-scope sources agree. Traube 2014 (CAPD, p. 8) is the primary and governs the specific cadence — CAPD performed a minimum of twice daily, once by each shift nurse — with Traube 2017 corroborating twice-daily each-shift CAPD screening (and citing the ESPNIC every-8-12-hour recommendation), and PANDEM 2022 endorsing routine delirium monitoring plus a nonpharmacologic (ICU Liberation) prevention bundle at guideline level. Curley 2006 is the nearest match on assessment frequency but a different intervention — the State Behavioral Scale's every-4-hour sedation-scoring cadence is not delirium rescreening — so it must not be read as direct support.

statement: Positive → rule out withdrawal (WAT-1); find and fix precipitants; bundle levers first — drugs treat symptoms only.
synthesis: The two on-scope sources agree fully: SCCM PANDEM 2022 (the governing PICU guideline) directs that initial delirium management target identifying and treating underlying etiologies (BRAIN MAPS), recommends WAT-1/SOS to assess iatrogenic withdrawal, and states antipsychotics "do not treat the cause(s)" — reserved for refractory/severe delirium and used only alongside/after low-risk nonpharmacologic measures; Traube 2017 independently prescribes the same sequence (assess precipitating illness, then iatrogenic causes including opiate withdrawal, then environment, with drugs only if the child remains delirious after these are addressed). PANDEM governs as the primary source and Traube 2017 concurs; the screening/arousal tools (CAPD, psCAM-ICU, pCAM-ICU, RASS) and the ICU Liberation bundle are cited as the assessment/bundle machinery, not the positive-result action steps, and Curley's SBS is a keyword-adjacent sedation scale (different intervention) that must not be read as support for the delirium-management statement.

statement: Target arousal (unit RASS / SBS goal for this child)
synthesis: The on-scope sources agree and govern: SCCM PANDEM 2022 (p. e83 / PDF p.10) recommends the SBS (strong) or RASS (conditional) to assess sedation level and suggests assigning a per-patient target depth of sedation using a validated tool at least daily, and Curley 2006 defines the SBS with the sedation goal of a calm but responsive state — together supporting a unit RASS/SBS arousal goal for the child. The delirium tools (Traube 2014 CAPD, Smith 2016 psCAM-ICU, Traube 2017) and the RASS source (Sessler 2002) share the RASS keyword but use it as an arousal gate or subtype descriptor for delirium screening/epidemiology, a different-intervention scope that should not be read as direct support for setting a sedation target.

statement: Sedation, analgesia & delirium plan for today
synthesis: The on-scope governing source is the SCCM PANDEM 2022 pediatric guideline, which directly frames the day's plan for the rounds-script line: it addresses sedation, pain (analgesia), and delirium together, recommends a validated-tool sedation target "at least once daily" plus protocolized sedation/analgesia, and routine delirium monitoring with validated tools. statement: Two-step: DTS → bCAM
synthesis: Han 2013 and the 2014 Geriatric ED Guidelines both explicitly define and recommend the sequential two-step DTS to bCAM approach - a highly sensitive rule-out screen (DTS) followed by a highly specific rule-in confirmation (bCAM); Han 2013 is the validation source that governs. The 2026 GED Guidelines 2.0 update endorses DTS to rule out and bCAM to rule in but lists them within a broader menu of instruments (4AT, CAM-ICU, mCAM, AMT-4, RASS) rather than re-mandating the specific DTS to bCAM sequence, so the two-step DTS to bCAM pathway remains the current position, consistent with (not overturned by) the 2026 update.

statement: bCAM directly
synthesis: Both sources agree and are complementary. The ED-DEL toolkit's Delirium Assessment Approach (Resource V-B) is the on-scope governing source for the "bCAM directly" pathway: it explicitly states that when screening only high-risk patients (age 65+ or a history of dementia), you skip the triage screen and "go straight to evaluation with a delirium-specific instrument... such as Brief Confusion Assessment Method (bCAM)." Han 2013 supplies the bCAM's validated characteristics (a "highly specific rule-in test" designed to be brief) and sanctions standalone use, noting the two-step model "can be tailored... one or both components can be used"; note Han designed the bCAM to be <1 minute, so the tool's "<2-minute" descriptor is a conservative rounding, not a conflict.

statement: 4AT
synthesis: All four sources agree that the 4AT is an appropriate rapid delirium screening instrument for the emergency department / acute setting: the 4AT v1.2 form defines the tool and its 0 / 1-3 / >=4 score bands, SIGN 157 gives a graded recommendation to use the 4AT in emergency department and acute hospital settings, NICE CG103 (2023) directs use of the 4AT when delirium indicators are present, and GED Guidelines 2.0 (2026) conditionally recommend the 4AT among ED delirium tools and note it has the largest ED evidence base. The on-scope ED recommendations govern; the different-scope nearest matches are boundary conditions rather than contradictions — SIGN's parallel community-setting recommendation and the NICE/SIGN critical-care carve-out that substitutes CAM-ICU/ICDSC for the 4AT in ICU/recovery, plus GED2's broader multi-setting review used as indirect evidence.

statement: Delirium Triage Screen — script "Say: “Can you spell the word LUNCH backwards?”"; RASS 0 and 0–1 errors → DTS negative — delirium less likely (98% sensitive rule-out). Continue clinical evaluation; rescreen with any change in mental status.
synthesis: Han 2013 is the on-scope ED validation that governs the card: it establishes the DTS script (spell LUNCH backwards), the RASS-0-plus-≤1-error negative threshold, and the 98% sensitivity rule-out, while the Vanderbilt DTS manual (the primaryAnchor, unarchived) supplies the operator script and the 'continue evaluation / rescreen with any change in mental status' guidance not found in the paper. The two sources agree on the core; the nearest different-scope matches within Han 2013 (an in-hospital non-ICU admitted subgroup, and the caveat that performance may differ in patients under 65) share keywords but do not replace the primary ED-bedside, ≥65 validation.

statement: 4AT — alertness + AMT4 + months-backward + acute change. Bands: ≥ 4: possible delirium ± cognitive impairment (≥4); 1–3: possible cognitive impairment (≥1); 0: delirium or severe cognitive impairment unlikely (≥0)
synthesis: All four sources agree on the 4AT's four items (alertness, AMT4, Months-Backward attention, acute change/fluctuating course) and its score bands. The 4AT v1.2 instrument (primary, on-scope) states the full three-band structure verbatim (≥4 possible delirium ± cognitive impairment; 1–3 possible cognitive impairment; 0 delirium/severe cognitive impairment unlikely), and Bellelli 2014 restates all three bands; Shenkin 2019 and Tieges 2021 corroborate the four items and the pre-specified ≥4 delirium cutoff. The instrument governs because the claim describes the tool's own structure, which is population- and setting-independent, so the validation studies (geriatric ward / acute medical inpatients / general first-presentation) reinforce rather than qualify it.

statement: Review medications first (new, changed, or deliriogenic drugs; anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids) and consider withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines).
synthesis: Both on-scope sources agree with the claim: ADEPT's evaluation guidance and the ADEPT-derived ED-DEL assessment protocol both direct the clinician to review medications for recent changes and high-risk/deliriogenic drugs and to assess alcohol/benzodiazepine use, with ADEPT Table 1 explicitly naming anticholinergics and benzodiazepines and listing "alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal." The one weakly-supported element is "opioids": neither source itemizes opioids in its deliriogenic list — support is only oblique (ADEPT's prevention step to prefer "nonsedating, nonopioid" analgesia), and the prevention/treatment passages that echo the same drug classes are a different-intervention scope (avoid/minimize) that does not govern this "look for the cause" statement.

statement: Screen for infection, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, metabolic derangement, and neurologic causes as clinically indicated.
synthesis: Both sources directly support screening delirium-positive older ED patients for underlying causes spanning infection, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, metabolic derangement, and neurologic conditions: the ADEPT 'Evaluate' step with its Table 1 of readily reversible causes names each category, and the ED-DEL toolkit's 'do not miss' conditions and focused workup corroborate the same list. statement: Check for pain, urinary retention, and constipation — common, reversible precipitants.
synthesis: Both ED-focused sources agree that pain, urinary retention, and constipation are common, reversible precipitants/contributors to look for in the older ED patient. The ED-DEL toolkit governs the exact wording: it names untreated pain, fecal impaction, and urinary retention together as serious causes and labels pain/constipation as factors that precipitate/exacerbate delirium, while ADEPT's Table 1 lists pain and urinary retention among readily reversible precipitants and addresses constipation as a bothersome symptom to treat — complementary, not conflicting, and all on-scope.

statement: Reorient frequently; involve family or a sitter; keep glasses and hearing aids on.
synthesis: Both cited sources agree and are on-scope for the older ED patient: ADEPT (p.7, the primary anchor) directs reorientation with large-font clocks/visual cues, family/caregiver calming presence and 1:1 sitters, and provision of hearing/vision aids (its Table 1 flags "lack of hearing or vision aids" as a precipitant), and the ED-DEL toolkit's ED delirium-prevention protocol independently directs family involvement in orienting, ensuring glasses and hearing aids are worn, self-orientation cues, and 1:1 sitters — so ADEPT governs as the primary source with the ED-DEL protocol corroborating every element. statement: Minimize tethers (catheters, telemetry, restraints) and disruptions; mobilize when safe.
synthesis: Both sources are ED-specific older-adult delirium guidance and agree directly with the claim: ADEPT's PREVENT step and the ACEP ED-DEL toolkit each instruct minimizing tethers (bladder/Foley catheters, monitor leads/telemetry, BP cuffs, IV lines), avoiding physical restraints, limiting unnecessary disruptions/vital-sign cycling, and promoting mobility (ambulation, up in a chair) when safe. statement: Document the screen result, the suspected causes, and the interventions started.
synthesis: The ED-DEL toolkit's ED-to-inpatient/SNF Delirium Transfer Checklist (p. 106-107) is the governing on-scope source and fully supports the statement: it explicitly records the screening test done and whether delirium is present (screen result), potential contributors identified on work-up (suspected causes), and prevention/management strategies implemented in the ED (interventions started). Han 2010 agrees only in part — it recommends uncovering the underlying etiology and notifying the next level of care of delirium status once delirium is diagnosed in the ED, but frames this as clinical management/handoff rather than a documentation step and does not address recording interventions, so it is a narrower, partial match; a same-source keyword collision ("Documenting Outcomes") concerns program-level QI data, a different scope.

statement: Hand the result off explicitly at disposition — delirium found in the ED changes inpatient management and follow-up.
synthesis: Both sources agree and are on-scope for older ED patients. The ED-DEL change package and toolkit (the primary source) directs clinicians to communicate delirium status explicitly to the inpatient MD and RN and at transitions of care from the ED to the next site (its Strategy 4 'Optimize communication' tactic on p.9, restated cleanly in the prevention/treatment protocol on p.99 and embodied in the ED-to-inpatient/SNF transfer checklist on p.107), and Han 2010 independently states that if admitted, physicians at the next level of care should be notified of the patient's delirium status, documenting that unrecognized ED delirium worsens the inpatient workup and post-discharge follow-up. The ED-DEL toolkit governs as the primary source and Han corroborates the disposition-handoff imperative.

statement: A positive screen in the ED independently predicts mortality — treat it as a finding that matters.

statement: Screen older ED patients per your department’s policy — most ED delirium is hypoactive and quiet, and is missed without a screen.
synthesis: The ED-specific sources agree: ADEPT 2020 (p.4, the primary anchor) and Han 2010 (p.8) state directly that most ED delirium is the hypoactive, "quiet" subtype (~90%) and is often missed without a formal assessment, while Han 2013 and GED Guidelines 2.0 corroborate high ED miss rates and support screening set by local/departmental protocol (GED 2.0 favors risk-stratified rather than universal screening). SIGN 157 also recommends the 4AT in the ED and agrees hypoactive delirium predominates, but NICE CG103 corroborates the same hypoactive-quiet-often-missed picture only for hospital/long-term care and explicitly flags the ED as a research gap, and the 4AT sheet is setting-general — so ADEPT, as the ED-specific source, governs.

statement: Score the RASS first. Any RASS other than 0 is altered arousal.
synthesis: Han 2013 governs and directly supports the claim: the Delirium Triage Screen scores the RASS (arousal) as its first component, and any RASS other than 0 is treated as altered level of consciousness/arousal; ADEPT (also ED) and GED Guidelines 2.0 — which cites the mRASS-other-than-0 cutpoint in older ED patients — corroborate on-scope. The nearest matches differ in scope and must not be read as direct support for the RASS≠0 rule: the 4AT gates on its own Alertness item rather than RASS, while SIGN 157, NICE CG103, and Han 2010 describe altered arousal or use other instruments (CAM-ICU) without defining the RASS-scored-first ED gate.

statement: RASS −4 / −5 → stupor / coma — record “unable to assess”; reassess when the patient responds to voice.
synthesis: The on-scope emergency-department sources agree: Han 2010 states directly that a patient must be arousable to verbal stimuli to assess for delirium (comatose patients are excluded), and the GED 2.0 DSM-5-TR criterion on p.2 confirms delirium cannot be diagnosed under severely reduced arousal such as coma; Han 2013 defines RASS -5 as coma/unarousable and ADEPT shows the DTS begins with a formal arousal assessment — together supporting "RASS -4/-5 → record unable to assess, reassess when the patient responds to voice," with Han 2010 governing as the most direct on-scope statement. synthesis: The on-scope ED sources agree that at disposition the delirium screen result should be handed off to the receiving team: ADEPT (the governing primary source, p.7) states the diagnosis must be communicated explicitly to the inpatient team, Han 2010 says physicians at the next level of care should be notified of the patient's delirium status, SIGN 157 directs documenting the diagnosis to aid transfers of care (handover notes, referral, discharge letters), and GED Guidelines 2.0 endorses exactly the named screens (4AT/bCAM to rule in-or-out, DTS to rule out) in older ED patients, with Han 2013 and the 4AT instrument supplying those tools and their result bands. statement: Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale, 10 levels: +4 Combative (overtly combative/violent; immediate danger to staff) … 0 Alert & calm … −5 Unarousable (no response to voice or physical stimulation).
synthesis: All four sources concern the same instrument, the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale, and the claim's exact 10-level enumeration with endpoint wording ("+4 Combative … immediate danger to staff", "0 Alert and calm", "−5 Unarousable … no response to voice or physical stimulation") is reproduced verbatim in Ely 2003 Table 1 (explicitly a "10point scale", originally derived by Sessler 2002), which is the on-scope governing source. Han 2015 — the card's primary citation — presents the same scale as its Figure 1 but studies it in older ED patients and relabels "sedation" as "drowsy," and Chester 2012 evaluates a modified RASS (mRASS) in VA medical inpatients, so both are nearest matches at a different scope rather than the source of the standard endpoint descriptors.

statement: Score arousal first (Look, then Talk, then Touch). It is the CAM-IMC’s level-of-consciousness item.

Han 2015 (the named primary anchor) and Chester 2012 agree in principle that RASS quantifies level of consciousness for delirium but are different-scope nearest matches (Han: ED, standalone screen; Chester: modified RASS in ward inpatients), so Beyer 2024 governs the CAM-IMC clause and Ely/Sessler govern the administration sequence; all sources are mutually consistent with no contradiction.

statement: RASS −4 / −5 → STOP — stupor or coma; the CAM-IMC cannot be scored now. Reassess when the patient responds to voice.
synthesis: The on-scope governing source is Beyer 2024 (CAM-IMC): it establishes the CAM-IMC as a verbal delirium test for non-intubated step-down patients that can only be applied when the patient is accessible to oral evaluation, which directly supports stopping and not scoring at RASS -4/-5 (stupor/coma), while the specific RASS thresholds and the 'responds to voice' reassessment trigger come from the Sessler 2002 scale definition. Han 2015 is the nearest match on RASS and arousal but is an ED study that used the RASS as a delirium screen and explicitly excluded comatose patients, so it is a different setting and a different use of the RASS and does not govern this arousal gate.

statement: A multicomponent non-pharmacologic bundle reduced incident delirium in non-ICU inpatients (Cochrane RR 0.69). Antipsychotics do NOT prevent delirium — do not use them prophylactically.
synthesis: The primary on-scope source, Siddiqi 2016 (Cochrane, hospitalised non-ICU patients), directly supports both prongs — multicomponent interventions cut incident delirium (RR 0.69) while antipsychotics as a class show no clear benefit — and it governs because it is the exact population and figure the claim cites; it is corroborated for the bundle by Inouye 1999 and Hshieh 2015 and for antipsychotics by Oh 2019 and Neufeld 2016. The only divergence is scope, not direction: atypical/second-generation antipsychotics reduced incidence in postoperative surgical trials (Siddiqi's olanzapine subgroup and Oh's second-generation pooled RR 0.36), and the AGS 2015 postoperative guideline rates prophylactic antipsychotics as "insufficient evidence" rather than clearly ineffective — a different surgical setting/agent that should not be read as endorsing routine antipsychotic prophylaxis in general non-ICU inpatients.

statement: Ten-component HELP-style bundle: reorientation; glasses & hearing aids; early mobilisation; sleep protocol; hydration & nutrition; deliriogenic/anticholinergic medication review; pain treated without over-sedation; bowel/bladder care; infection/hypoxia/metabolic work-up; family engagement & education.
synthesis: All four sources support a HELP-style multicomponent nonpharmacological prevention bundle for hospitalised older adults and none contradicts the claim: the AGS 2015 postoperative-delirium guideline (primary anchor, p. 4) governs the specific list, enumerating nearly all ten components in one strong recommendation, while Inouye 1999 (HELP) and Hshieh 2015 establish and meta-analytically validate the core six (reorientation, sleep, mobilisation, vision/hearing, hydration) and Siddiqi 2016 confirms multicomponent prevention works in the exact hospitalised non-ICU (step-down) setting. The four extra components (medication review, pain without over-sedation, bowel/bladder care, infection/hypoxia/metabolic work-up, family engagement) rest chiefly on the AGS enumeration — drawn from an older-surgical population — rather than on all four sources, so the AGS list is the governing citation for the full ten while the HELP trials cover only the core six.

statement: Review deliriogenic / anticholinergic medications first — minimise the burden.
synthesis: Both sources endorse reviewing and minimising deliriogenic/anticholinergic medications to reduce delirium. Lisibach 2022 is the on-scope, governing source for a general step-down/ward card: in older hospitalised (non-ICU) patients a high cumulative anticholinergic burden was independently associated with incident delirium, and discontinuing or substituting high-burden drugs is presented as a targeted preventive intervention (with the caveat that drugs are only one factor in a multifactorial syndrome). AGS 2015 corroborates the same principle — a strong recommendation to avoid anticholinergic/deliriogenic drugs and to evaluate medications to identify causes — but from a different population (postoperative older surgical patients), so it is a nearest-match at a different scope rather than direct on-scope support.

section: Act card — Manage without new harm
statement: Apply the multicomponent non-pharmacologic bundle — first-line for every patient.
synthesis: All three sources agree that a multicomponent non-pharmacologic bundle is the recommended, harm-free first-line intervention for delirium; Siddiqi 2016 — the only source covering hospitalised non-ICU medical and surgical wards, the closest match to a step-down setting — governs and concludes these interventions should be adopted into routine care. The supporting evidence is strongest for primary prevention in at-risk patients (Inouye's HELP RCT was in older ≥70 general-medicine inpatients; AGS gives a strong prevention recommendation but only a weak one for treating established postoperative delirium), so "first-line for every patient" is a reasonable extrapolation of the consensus rather than a directly tested claim.

section: Act card — Manage without new harm
statement: Antipsychotics do NOT prevent or treat delirium — do not use them routinely.
synthesis: All three systematic reviews agree that current evidence does not support the routine use of antipsychotics to prevent (Oh 2019) or treat (Nikooie 2019) delirium in hospitalized adults, and the primary source, Neufeld 2016 — which addresses both indications — reaches the same conclusion, so the card statement is well grounded and governed by Neufeld 2016. The only qualifications are nearest-match subgroups that must not be read as endorsement: Oh 2019's limited-evidence finding that second-generation antipsychotics (not haloperidol) may lower delirium incidence specifically in postoperative surgical patients, Nikooie 2019's palliative-care signal of net harm, and Neufeld 2016's caveat that none of the trials evaluated short-term symptomatic relief of agitation/distress.

statement: Reserve short-term, low-dose antipsychotics only for severe agitation endangering the patient.

NICE's treatment recommendation (marked 2010, amended 2022) remains the current position because the 2023 NICE update re-addressed only assessment and diagnosis; the nearest-match paragraphs on prophylactic/preventive antipsychotics (AGS section X, NICE research recommendation 2) share the 'antipsychotic' keyword but concern prevention rather than treatment of agitation and must not be read as support.

statement: Apply the multicomponent non-pharmacologic prevention bundle to every at-risk patient, every shift.
synthesis: All three sources agree that a multicomponent, risk-factor–targeted nonpharmacologic bundle reduces incident delirium in at-risk hospitalised non-ICU patients: the Cochrane 2016 review (RR 0.69, effect similar in medical and surgical settings) is the most directly on-scope source and governs the general step-down setting, underpinned by the Inouye 1999 HELP RCT (older medical patients) and the AGS 2015 strong recommendation (at-risk older surgical patients). Two caveats warrant flagging: the claim's "every shift" cadence is an operational specification — the sources specify daily rounds, three-times-daily protocols, "the entire hospitalization," and "re-orientation at frequent intervals" rather than literally every shift — and Cochrane's pharmacologic/anaesthetic prevention findings (antipsychotics with no clear effect; BIS-guided anaesthesia positive) are different interventions that share the "prevent delirium" keyword but must not be read as support for the nonpharmacologic bundle.

perSource.note: Cochrane review of interventions for preventing delirium in hospitalised non-ICU patients — the most directly on-scope source for a general step-down (non-ICU) setting; pooled RCT evidence that the multicomponent nonpharmacologic bundle reduces incident delirium.

statement: Negative → document it; normal arousal does not exclude delirium — rescreen with any change.
synthesis: The two sources are complementary rather than conflicting: Beyer 2024 — validated in the intermediate/step-down care setting the tool targets — is the on-scope source for "normal arousal does not exclude delirium," because the CAM-IMC's point-based scoring makes the altered-arousal item non-mandatory so a fully alert (RASS 0) patient can still screen positive, while NICE CG103 governs "document it" and "rescreen with any change" through its daily-observation, assess-on-change and record-in-notes recommendations (for the broader hospital/long-term-care population). The nearest NICE match to the arousal point is its hypoactive-delirium vigilance guidance, which concerns reduced — not normal — arousal and should not be read as direct support for that clause.

statement: Positive → find the cause (review meds first), manage without new harm, and hand the finding off.
synthesis: The on-scope guidance agrees on the workflow. NICE CG103 governs this "act on a positive" step: identify and manage the underlying cause(s) (including medication review), de-escalate non-pharmacologically first with only cautious short-term haloperidol if needed, and document the diagnosis in the person's notes and primary-care record (the hand-off). AGS 2015 concurs on identifying/managing the cause and avoiding harmful sedatives, restraints and non-indicated antipsychotics/benzodiazepines, though its population is postoperative older adults; Lisibach 2022 supports "review meds first" specifically for anticholinergic burden in non-ICU older inpatients (narrower). Siddiqi 2016 is the nearest match on multi-component/medication approaches but addresses prevention rather than acting on a positive screen — a different-intervention scope, so it does not govern this claim.

statement: RASS −4/−5 — stupor or coma. Record it, and reassess when the patient responds to voice.
synthesis: Neither cited source states the claim's gating rule verbatim: the direct authority for the RASS -4/-5 arousal threshold (stupor/coma, unarousable) and the "responds to voice" cue for resuming assessment is Sessler 2002 (RASS), the web source, which governs here. Beyer 2024 (the CAM-IMC step-down validation named as primary anchor) only corroborates that the setting uses RASS/level-of-consciousness and defines RASS -5 as deeply sedated; its keyword-adjacent passages - aggressive patients who could not be examined, and verbal testing only when patients are accessible to oral evaluation - are different-scope and must not be read as direct support.

perSource.note: CAM-IMC validation in non-intubated cardiac-surgery step-down patients; corroborates that the setting uses RASS/level-of-consciousness and defines RASS -5 as deeply sedated, but never states the RASS -4/-5 unable-to-assess record-and-reassess-on-voice gate.
